catalog_quote: [Jacques et al. 2012 p.1100] Syllables in polysyllabic words may be stressed or unstressed. In verb forms, the verb stem is always stressed, as is the first syllable of a bi- or tri-syllabic suffix string. Given its predictable nature in verb forms, stress is not indicated in the present paper. ... [Jacques 2016 sec. 2] Khaling has a two-way tonal contrast on open syllables with long vowels or closed syllables with a sonorant coda. There is a high level tone (indicated by a macron) and a falling tone (circumflex accent). ... The tonal contrast is neutralized on short and / or unstressed vowels. ... In polysyllables, only stressed syllables receive tone, and verbs and nouns alike only have one stressed syllable, except in the case of compound verbs, which are not discussed in this paper. ... audit.reasoning: The deciding quotations are verbatim in the held files at the stated locators (Jacques et al. 2012 p.1100 sec. 3; Jacques 2016 sec. 2, HAL pp.4-5; Toba 1979 sec. 1.4). The classification 'morphological' (verb stem always stressed regardless of prefixes; one stress per word; tone contrast licensed only on the stressed syllable) follows directly from the quoted text. The sources are the modern first-hand descriptions by the team that documented Khaling (2012 journal article with a phonology section; 2016 phonology chapter), and no reference grammar, JIPA illustration, dissertation or instrumental prosody study of Khaling was found in Glottolog, HAL, Crossref or archive.org; two further open Jacques items fetched sources now (2015 verb dictionary, 2015 derivational morphology) are silent on stress.
